abstract.p: Fluoride contamination in coastal aquifers is difficult to evaluate because its mobilisation is controlled by overlapping and seasonally dynamic non-stationary hydrogeochemical processes influenced by seawater intrusion, lithological heterogeneity, recharge, and anthropogenic activity. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and apply an integrated, uncertainty-aware framework to identify the dominant processes controlling groundwater fluoride, quantify their relative contributions, and relate them to lithology and land use factors. To address these complexities, a Bayesian-Absolute Principal Component Scores-Multiple Linear Regression (APCS–MLR) receptor model, integrated with Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), was proposed to achieve uncertainty-aware source apportionment. Data-informed priors combined with prior–posterior checks and No-U-Turn Sampler-based (NUTS) inference produced credible, physically consistent source contribution intervals within the Bayesian model. The framework was applied to an underexplored eastern coastal aquifer system of India, where seasonal monitoring of 171 stations revealed emerging F- hotspots with concentrations up to 7.10 mg/L, raising concerns among water authorities. The proposed Bayesian APCS–MLR receptor model revealed that groundwater fluoride was overwhelmingly controlled by geogenic leaching during the pre-monsoon season (89.14%, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): 80.09–97.26%), with only minor contributions from pH modulation (4.48%, CI: 0.32–9.19%) and silicate weathering/cation exchange (1.24%, CI: 0.12–2.39%), while anthropogenic and salinity influences remained negligible (0.23%, CI: 0.01–0.65% and 0.14%, CI: 0.01–0.42%, respectively). In the post-monsoon season, geogenic control weakened substantially to 48.86% (95% CI: 38.80–64.91%), concurrent with stronger recharge-enhanced pH effects (16.13%, CI: 3.20–24.11%) and intensified ion-exchange contributions (3.83%, CI: 0.75–7.31%). Unidentified contributions also rose sharply to 30.03% (CI: 24.72–33.68%) during post-monsoon, indicating the growing role of mixing, complexation, and unresolved non-linear mechanisms under post-monsoon conditions. Posterior probability distributions further showed that seasonal fluoride variability is primarily governed by recharge-driven processes superimposed on a persistent geogenic baseline, with lithology and land use acting as dominant regulators. Fine-textured formations and cropland or plantation areas retained strong geogenic influence, whereas coarse alluvium and aquaculture-linked settings exhibited stronger post-monsoon anthropogenic pH- and ion-exchange-driven fluoride release, likely facilitated by aquaculture pond leakage and clay compaction. Overall, the proposed methodology offers an uncertainty-aware and process-informed approach for source identification and apportionment in complex aquifers with overlapping hydrogeochemical controls, supporting informed groundwater management under SDG 6.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Achieving Sustainable Development Goal 6 mandates access to safe drinking water, yet geogenic groundwater contaminants like fluoride (F-) remain pervasive. Globally, more than 200 million people are exposed to high F-, including about 120 million in India1–3. Chronic exposure beyond the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline of 1.5 mg/L causes dental and skeletal fluorosis, anaemia, and gastrointestinal disorders4. In India, high F- groundwater is common in inland hard-rock aquifers of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu, with levels often above 1.5 mg/L and occasionally exceeding 5 mg/L5–8. Elevated concentrations are also reported in coastal aquifers 0.6–1.8 mg/L in Andhra Pradesh9, up to 3.3 mg/L in Thoothukudi (Tamil Nadu)10, and 0.06–3.51 mg/L in Bharuch (Gujarat)11, making fluoride contamination a growing concern along India’s 11,000 Kilometre coastline12.

Coastal aquifer geochemistry is complex, non-linear, and seasonally dynamic. Seawater intrusion and evapoconcentration raise ionic strength and pH while reducing Ca2⁺ through Na–Ca exchange and carbonate precipitation1,13. These changes enhance fluorite solubility and weaken F- adsorption, often producing non-linear relationships with salinity, pH, and Ca2⁺1. Salinisation complicates remediation as competing anions hinder adsorption, precipitation method depends on Ca2⁺ and pH, and desalination demands strict antiscalant use and safe brine disposal14. Added variability from tidal pumping and monsoonal recharge creates non-stationary conditions, undermining one-time assessments and fixed designs for remediation15. Balasore in northern Odisha is one of the most vulnerable coastal regions of India, where geological layering, saline water dynamics, and human activity elevate fluoride risk. The aquifer comprises fractured basement, thick alluvium, and laterite, with brackish shallow and fresher deeper zones that shift seasonally16. Agricultural and aquaculture practices add alkalinity and competing anions that may mobilise F- and weaken treatment performance17. The region is socio-economically backward, cyclone-prone, and heavily reliant on groundwater for domestic and agricultural use. Moreover, earlier F- exceedances were documented in Nilgiri, Remuna, and Bhograi blocks16,18, while current study shows new hotspots appearing in Patrajhada (Basta), Machhua (Nilgiri), Chandipur (Balasore Sadar) and Rupsa regions. These evolving conditions highlight the need to unravel overlapping geochemical processes that drive fluoride enrichment in this coastal system.

Fluoride geochemistry in coastal aquifers, particularly in Eastern India, remains poorly documented and insufficiently understood. Existing studies have largely relied on single-season datasets, basic or conventional statistical tools, and broad hydrochemical interpretation, which are often inadequate for resolving the non-linear, overlapping, and seasonally dynamic controls operating in coastal systems. Although fluoride occurrence has been reported, the relative roles of salinisation, ion exchange, carbonate reactions, lithological influence, land-use effects, and anthropogenic alkalinity have rarely been quantitatively separated, while land-use and anthropogenic drivers themselves remain insufficiently explored9,11,19–24. In addition, uncertainty-aware, process-level attribution has seldom been attempted, limiting the development of targeted and reliable remediation strategies. These gaps restrict informed intervention, particularly in dynamic coastal environments where hydrochemical conditions vary strongly over space and time25–31.

Against this background, the present study develops an integrative, process-based framework to overcome these shortcomings and advance previous works in four key ways. First, it uses a multi-season hydrochemical dataset to capture the temporal variability of fluoride behaviour under monsoonal recharge and salinity shifts. Second, geochemical evaluation based on ionic ratios, correlation analysis, and saturation index assessment is integrated with Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) and K-means clustering to identify hydrochemical regimes while preserving the mixed, non-Gaussian, and non-linear structure typical of coastal groundwater systems32. Third, PCA with varimax rotation is applied to resolve interpretable geochemical controls linked to fluorite dissolution, salinisation, ion exchange, and anthropogenic alkalinity. Fourth, and most importantly, a novel Bayesian Absolute Principal Component Score–Multiple Linear Regression (Bayesian-APCS-MLR) receptor model is proposed to quantify the contributions of overlapping controls with explicit uncertainty characterization. Unlike Chemical Mass Balance (CMB), the Bayesian model does not require fixed source fingerprints33; compared with UNMIX and frequentist APCS-MLR, it is less sensitive to collinearity through the use of priors and provides posterior credible intervals and dominance probabilities34. Unlike Positive Matrix Factorisation (PMF), which commonly relies on bootstrap and displacement diagnostics35, the Bayesian approach directly yields posterior uncertainty distributions that are more informative for water quality management. Together, these advances move beyond occurrence-based assessment and provide an uncertainty-aware, management-oriented framework for understanding fluoride mobilisation in a complex and seasonally dynamic coastal aquifer.

Overall, the proposed framework unravels the multiple controls on coastal fluoride mobilisation based on machine learning/statistical modelling and correlation analysis with lithologic as well as land use pattern, quantifies their contributions with uncertainty based on proposed Bayesian receptor model. It enables process-specific remediation strategies aligned with dominant mechanisms across different hydrogeochemical zones. Its tolerance for non-Gaussian chemistry and uncertainty-aware attribution makes it transferable to other complex aquifers, including monsoon deltas, arid coasts, volcanic terrains, and island systems where overlapping factors like, ionic strength, alkalinity, and Ca2⁺ scarcity govern fluoride risk simultaneously. As a response-agnostic methodology, it can also be adopted to other geogenic hazards such as arsenic, nitrate, and salinity, where mixed sources and seasonal variability challenge conventional management.

sec.title: Details of location and climatic conditions
sec.p:
The study site is located in Balasore district, positioned along the north-eastern coastline of Odisha, India (Fig. 1a). Geographically, it spans from approximately 21°03’ to 21°59’ North latitude and 86°20’ to 87°29’ East longitude, covering an area of about 3,806 square kilometers. The groundwater resources are highly utilized in the district, with Bhograi block being the highest (68.77%) and Nilgiri block the lowest (32.42%) with respect to overall groundwater utilization estimation16. The study area falls under sub-tropical climate characterized by high temperature and high humidity. The annual average rainfall is 1568 mm, which is mainly contributed by south-west monsoon.Fig. 1
(a) Map of Balasore district showing major water bodies, including prominent river basins and drainage networks16, along with the locations of groundwater sampling sites; Geospatial distribution of F−concentration in groundwater of the region during (b) pre-monsoon and (c) post-monsoon season.

sec.title: Hydrogeology and geomorphology
sec.p: The drainage in the study area is mainly governed by rivers like Budhabalanga, Sono, Subarnarekha, and Kansabans, which flow into the Bay of Bengal (Fig. 1a). Geographically, the region comprises inner alluvial plains, southwestern hills, and a coastal belt shaped by erosional, fluvio-marine, and depositional processes. The coastal plains are of fluvio-marine origin, while the alluvial plains result from fluvial activity16 (Fig. 1a). River flows are minimal in lean seasons and peak during monsoon. Geologically, the area lies within the Singhbhum craton and includes Archaeo-Proterozoic basement rocks and recent alluvium (Fig. S1, Table S1). The lithology comprises granite gneiss, granophyre, dolerite, and laterites, with aquifers in coastal regions formed of sand, silt, and clay, and in hard rock areas from weathered and fractured zones (Fig. S1). Groundwater flows from northwest to southeast, discharging into the Bay of Bengal, with water table depths typically between 6–8 m bgl16.

sec.title: Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) of the study area
sec.p: The LULC of Balasore is dominated by agriculture, with cropland alone covering 2,490.37 sq km over 70% of the district forming a continuous belt across the central and southern alluvial plains (Fig. S2). Fertile clay–loam soils and extensive surface irrigation support multi-season paddy and other crops. Built-up land spans 552.93 sq km of urban and 4.53 sq km of rural areas, concentrated around Balasore city, Chandipur township, and along NH-16/NH-60, where industrial and service hubs form a spine of compact urban clusters. Forest cover is anchored by 295.72 sq km of deciduous forest with additional scrub and plantations, concentrated in the Nilgiri–Kuldiha hills. Coastal wetlands (74.66 sq km), mangroves/swamps (55.34 sq km), and aquaculture ponds dominate the shoreline, especially in Bhograi and Baliapal blocks. Inland water bodies (rivers, tanks, canals) account for 80.48 sq km, supporting both agriculture and aquaculture. Sandy and degraded scrublands occur as scattered clusters along beaches and river courses, while mining and quarrying (28.75 sq km) appear near Nilgiri, Khaira, and Soro blocks (Bhuvan NLCD: https://bhuvan.nrsc.gov.in).

sec.title: Sampling strategy and chemical analysis
sec.p: Groundwater samples were collected during both the pre-monsoon (n = 171) and post-monsoon (n = 171) seasons of 2022. On-site measurements of pH, Electrical Conductivity (EC), and Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) were performed using a HANNA multi-parameter probe. The device provides a pH accuracy of ± 0.02 units and an EC accuracy of 0.5% at 25 °C. Water samples were collected in 1L High Density Poly Ethylene (HDPE) containers that were thoroughly rinsed with double-distilled water prior to use. Groundwater was sampled from dug wells (10–30 m deep) in the coastal region, tube wells (35–70 m) in the alluvial plains, and bore wells (90–140 m) in the hard rock terrain. Prior to sampling, stagnant water was purged from the wells until a stable water temperature was observed, ensuring collection of fresh groundwater.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Normality tests (Shapiro–Wilk and Anderson–Darling) revealed that F- concentrations in both pre- and post-monsoon seasons deviate from a normal distribution. Consequently, the non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was applied to assess seasonal differences in median F- levels using PAST v. 5.2. Correlation matrices for both seasons were also generated using the same software.

To reduce dimensionality and extract dominant hydrogeochemical patterns, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was applied to the standardized groundwater chemistry dataset. Data were z-score normalized to ensure uniform scaling across variables. Five principal components were retained based on scree plot inflection, cumulative variance explained, and geochemical interpretability. Loadings were computed to evaluate the contribution of each variable, and orthogonal Varimax rotation was subsequently applied to improve component clarity. The number of iterations required for convergence of the Varimax algorithm was explicitly calculated. This yielded a simplified structure in which each component was more distinctly associated with specific hydrogeochemical processes such as pH controlling processes, silicate weathering, geogenic salinity or geogenic fluoride enrichment, and anthropogenic influence. Variables with rotated loadings ≥ 0.4 (absolute) were considered significant contributors. Heatmaps of rotated loadings were used for visual interpretation. All analyses were performed in Python using the scikit-learn library in Google Colab environment.

sec.title: Application of self -organising maps (SOM)
sec.p: Self-Organizing Map (SOM), an unsupervised neural network technique, was applied to classify groundwater quality based on twelve hydrogeochemical parameters: pH, TH, TDS, Mg2⁺, Ca2⁺, K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻, F-, HCO₃⁻, SO₄2⁻, and NO₃⁻. SOM enables dimensionality reduction by mapping high-dimensional data onto a two-dimensional grid while preserving topological relationships32. Data were first standardized using z-score normalization to ensure equal weight for all parameters. Probable SOM grid dimensions were generated by first estimating an optimal neuron count as five times the square root of the sample size (5√N) and then deriving an initial square grid whose side length is the integer part of √(5√N). To accommodate slight deviations from a perfect square, this base side was incrementally adjusted by ± 2 units to propose alternative widths (gx), with corresponding heights (gy) computed by dividing the target neuron count by each gx. Only those (gx, gy) combinations whose total nodes fell within ± 20% of the ideal neuron count were retained, ensuring both flexibility and fidelity to the desired map size. Finally, the surviving grid shapes were ordered by how closely their area matched the target, producing a ranked list of nearly square layouts for robust SOM training. Neighbourhood functions (Gaussian, Bubble, and Mexican-hat) were evaluated for their performance in minimizing Quantization Error (QE) and Topographic Error (TE). Total number of iterations along with learning rate (lr) and width of the neighbourhood function (σ) to be considered were also tuned to obtain minimum QE + TE value.

The Clustering of the hydrogeochemical groups were performed using k-means, and the optimal number of clusters was identified using the Elbow and Calinski-Harabasz index (CHI) methods. Dominant variables dictating cluster properties were determined by averaging chemistry within each cluster and converting to z-scores against the seasonal dataset mean and standard deviation. Variables with |z|≥ 1 were termed as dominant with sign (positive/negative) indicating increase or decrease compared to the overall mean.

The selected SOM structure generated visual outputs including component planes, U-matrix, and cluster maps. Component planes revealed spatial variation and inter-parameter relationships, while the U-matrix highlighted zones of similarity or transition. The final cluster map delineated distinct groundwater facies, aiding hydrogeochemical interpretation. SOM analysis was conducted in Python using the MiniSom library37 while the K-means clustering calculations were performed in scikit-learn and matplotlib Python packages.

sec.title: Source apportionment using Bayesian-absolute principal component scores—multiple linear regression (APCS-MLR)
sec.p: The retained principal components (PCs) were examined for multicollinearity using variance inflation factor (VIF)–like scores.

The methodological framework adopted in this study (Fig. 2) was selected for its reproducibility, interpretability, and practical suitability for hydrogeochemically dynamic coastal aquifers. In such settings, where groundwater chemistry is shaped by interacting seasonal, lithological, and anthropogenic controls, the use of standardized hydrochemical analysis and well-defined analytical steps ensures that the workflow can be applied consistently and independently reproduced. At the same time, the integration of statistical evaluation, self-organising maps, Bayesian APCS-MLR source apportionment, and geological and land-use information enables complex multivariate patterns to be translated into physically meaningful and environmentally plausible interpretations. This combined approach therefore provides a traceable basis for identifying dominant hydrochemical processes, quantifying source contributions with uncertainty, and relating observed groundwater-quality variations to their likely controlling factors.Fig. 2
End-to-end workflow of the Bayesian-APCS-MLR model proposed in the current study.

sec.title: Geology and LULC class extraction for the sampling locations
sec.p: A spatial overlay analysis was performed to characterize the local LULC and lithological setting around groundwater monitoring points. Shapefiles of LULC (Fig. S2) (Source: https://bhuvan-app1.nrsc.gov.in/2dresources/bhuvanstore.php) and lithological units (Fig. S1) (Source: https://bhukosh.gsi.gov.in/Bhukosh/MapViewer.aspx) were validated, assigned appropriate coordinate reference systems, and projected to Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) for accurate distance-based operations. Sample locations from cluster datasets were geocoded and attributed with at-point LULC and geology using polygon overlays, with an intersects fallback for edge cases. A 500 m buffer was generated around each point, and intersecting LULC and geological classes were extracted to compute class-wise areas and their percentage shares within each buffer zone. The geopandas, pyogrio, shapely, pyproj, rtree, pandas etc. python packages were used in Google Colab environment.

sec.title: General groundwater quality of the region
sec.p: The statistical distribution of groundwater chemistry is illustrated using box-whisker plots in Fig. S3, while Table S2 presents a comparison of the concentrations with WHO (2011)43 drinking water standards. The observed ionic dominance followed the sequence; Na⁺ > Mg2⁺ > K⁺ > Ca2⁺ for cations and HCO₃⁻ > SO₄2⁻ > Cl⁻ > NO₃⁻ for anions, suggesting a combination of geogenic, saline water influence and probable anthropogenic contributions. The F- levels in groundwater varied between 0.02 and 6.50 mg/L (avg. 1.15 mg/L) during the pre-monsoon season, and between 0.06 and 7.10 mg/L (avg. 1.24 mg/L) during post-monsoon period, as presented in Table S2. The seasonal variability is illustrated using box- whisker plots in Fig. S4a. Approximately 27% of pre-monsoon and 30% of post-monsoon samples exceeded the WHO (2011) permissible limit of 1.5 mg/L for drinking water (Figs. S4b,c). The spatial distribution of F- concentrations is mapped in Fig. 1b. Elevated F- levels exceeding the permissible limit were observed in groundwater from early reported fluoride endemic regions, including Patripal Panchayat (Remuna Block), Jayrampur Panchayat (Bhograi Block), Rupsa town, etc. while, newly developed fluoride contaminated zones were identified in Patrajhada Panchayat (Basta Block), Machhua (Nilgiri Block), and Chandipur (Balasore Sadar Block) regions.

The depth variation of fluoride concentration in the study area is presented in Figure S25. The figure shows that high fluoride values (> 1 mg/L) are mostly constrained to the shallow aquifer system while the deep aquifer systems are mostly showing values within 1 mg/L value. The seasonal variation in depth profile of fluoride concentration in the study area remain stable during pre- to post-monsoon transition (Fig. S25).

sec.title: Geochemical evaluation of groundwater system
sec.p: Gibbs diagrams (ratios of Na⁺/(Na⁺ + Ca2⁺) and Cl⁻/(Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) vs. TDS) indicate that groundwater samples from the study area predominantly cluster within rock–water interaction zone, with limited influence from evaporation (Fig. S5a, Fig. S5b). Furthermore, the Na+ normalised Mg2+ (µM/µM) and Na+ normalised HCO3- (µM/µM) vs. Na+ normalised Ca2+ plots show that majority of the samples during pre- and post-monsoon season are influenced by silicate weathering followed by minor evaporite dissolution and carbonate mineral weathering (Fig. S6a and Fig. S6b). Chadha’s modified Piper diagram in Fig. S7a, Fig. S7b reveals that groundwater mainly corresponds to Ca–Mg–HCO₃, Ca–Mg–Cl, Na–Cl, and Na–HCO₃ types (fields 5–8), with Ca–Mg–HCO₃ dominant, especially during post-monsoon season (Fig. S7b). Samples exceeding F- concentration 1.5 mg/L mostly belong to Ca–Mg–HCO₃ and Na–HCO₃ types. Pre-monsoon fluoride geochemistry is associated with fluoride mineral dissolution and natural softening processes, whereas post-monsoon conditions reflect dominant impact of freshwater recharge, facilitating fluoride mobilisation (Fig. S7a, Fig. S7b). Chloro-Alkaline Indices (CAI I & II) indicate natural softening as the dominant ion exchange process (65% of samples), with about 35% showing reverse ion exchange in both seasons (Fig. S8a, Fig. S8b).

Figure S9 illustrates the correlation coefficients between F- and key groundwater parameters during the pre- and post-monsoon seasons, while Figures S10, Fig. S11, Fig. S12 further examine these relationships through bivariate scatter plots. Most groundwater samples in the study area exhibit alkaline conditions, which are generally considered favorable for fluoride mobilization into groundwater44; however, the very weak correlations between HCO₃⁻ and F- (0.02 and 0.04 during pre- and post-monsoon, respectively) suggest that alkalinity alone does not exert a strong control on fluoride release, or that its influence is masked by other geochemical processes. Overall, correlation analysis shows weak or negligible associations between F- and most major water quality parameters (generally < 0.20 in both seasons), including EC (− 0.05 and − 0.09 during pre- and post-monsoon, respectively), indicating that fluoride occurrence is likely localized rather than governed by widespread salinization or regional rock–water interaction.

These findings are further supported by the scatter plots, which show no clear or consistent relationships between F- and major cations such as Ca2⁺, Mg2⁺, and Na⁺ (Fig. S10), and only limited salinity-related fluoride enrichment in a small subset of samples in the Cl⁻ vs. F- plots (Fig. S11a, b). Likewise, the HCO₃⁻ vs. F- plots (Fig. S11c, d) display clustered and complex distributions with only a few samples showing positive trends, while the SO₄2⁻ vs. F- plots (Fig. S11e, f) indicate no meaningful relationship in either season. The F- versus NO₃⁻ and K⁺ plots (Fig. S12a–d) show scattered patterns and multiple trends, particularly during the post-monsoon period, suggesting that anthropogenic inputs may influence fluoride behavior in some locations. In addition, the Kruskal–Wallis test results (Table S3) indicate no significant seasonal difference in groundwater fluoride median values, implying that overall fluoride concentrations in the study area are not substantially altered by temporal changes related to rainfall infiltration and associated seasonal geochemical variations.

sec.title: Mineralogical controls on fluoride geochemistry
sec.p: During the pre-monsoon period, prolonged dryness and increased groundwater residence time enhance the dissolution of silicate and evaporite minerals, elevating Na⁺ concentrations and groundwater alkalinity. Elevated alkalinity and pH promote calcite (CaCO₃) precipitation, which reduces dissolved Ca2⁺ availability. The resulting Ca2⁺ deficiency drives fluorite (CaF₂) dissolution via the common ion effect, increasing fluoride (F-) concentrations. Conversely, during the monsoon season, fresh recharge enriched with Ca2⁺ and Mg2⁺ shifts groundwater chemistry towards the Ca–Mg–HCO₃ type. Increased Ca2⁺ levels due to reverse ion exchange and freshwater recharge inhibit fluorite dissolution, resulting in more uniform F- levels throughout the region post-monsoon.

Additionally, natural softening process indicated in Figure S8 removes Ca2⁺ via groundwater softening, further promoting localized F- leaching. However, complex geochemical interactions involving carbonate chemistry, silicate weathering, evaporation, and changing groundwater residence time complicate any simple correlation between Ca2⁺ and F- concentrations, influencing fluoride enrichment dynamics significantly.

The role of pH, Ca2+ and alkalinity driving fluoride geochemistry is more evident based on the seasonal variation of SI values of the common fluoride and calcium minerals. The SI values of fluorite (SIFluorite) ranged from − 4.59 to 0.70 (avg. − 1.42) during pre-monsoon, and − 4.76 to 0.35 (avg. − 1.37) during post-monsoon periods (Table S4). SIFluorite vs. F- plots indicate increasing SI with rising fluoride levels (Fig. S13a, Fig. S14a), approaching equilibrium faster in the pre-monsoon season due to relatively higher alkalinity and longer residence times44. The SIFluorite vs. SICalcite plots show most samples undersaturated with respect to fluorite, favouring further dissolution (Fig. S13b, Fig. S14b). Higher F- samples, especially pre-monsoon, tend to be saturated or supersaturated with calcite, promoting Ca2⁺ removal via precipitation, thus facilitating fluoride release through fluorite dissolution. Limited and localized positive SIFluorite values indicate incipient fluorite re-precipitation processes. Comparing SIGypsum with SIFluorite (Fig. S13c, Fig. S14c), most high F- samples remain undersaturated for both minerals without consistent correlation with only few samples of very high fluoride concentration exhibiting incipient fluorite saturation. Interaction between dolomite saturation and fluorite behaviour shows many samples are dolomite-saturated but fluorite-undersaturated (Fig. S13d, Fig. S14d), especially during post-monsoon indicating increased Ca2⁺/Mg2⁺ concentrations and Ca–Mg–HCO₃ facies prevalence. Dolomite saturation may further remove Ca2⁺, enhancing fluorite dissolution and increasing groundwater fluoride concentrations.

sec.title: Source identification and apportionment of groundwater fluoride contamination
Major hydrological groups based on SOM and statistical modelling
sec.p: Optimisation of the grid size in SOM yielded (8 × 8) structure with minimum QE + TE values during both pre- and post-monsoon season. The gaussian neighbouring function with σ = 1.5, lr = 0.1, number of iterations = 32,000 and σ = 1.5, lr = 0.5, number of iterations = 64,000 were found to be optimised hyperparameters during pre- and post-monsoon seasons respectively.

The generated weight planes of the 12 input parameters during both pre-and post-monsoon seasons are presented in Fig. 3a & Fig. 3b respectively. In SOM output, neurons are represented using a colour gradient where reddish shades correspond to higher values of a given hydrogeochemical parameter, and blueish shades represent lower values.Fig. 3
(a) Pre-monsoon Self-Organizing Map (SOM) component planes for hydrochemical parameters (8 × 8 grid) displaying normalized neuron weights for pH, TDS, TH, Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, K+, Cl-, HCO₃⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄2⁻, and F-, respectively. (b) Post-monsoon Self-Organizing Map (SOM) component planes for hydrochemical parameters (8 × 8 grid) displaying normalized neuron weights for pH, TDS, TH, Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, K+, Cl-, HCO₃⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄2⁻, and F-, respectively.

The pH weight planes for pre-monsoon (Fig. 3a) exhibit deep-red coloration primarily in the top-left (TL) and bottom-left (BL) regions. In the post-monsoon period (Fig. 3b), the red area in TL expands, the BL region shifts from red to blue, and new red neurons emerge in the bottom-right (Bottom Right). These temporal changes indicate localized increases in groundwater pH due to monsoonal recharge, possibly driven by enhanced carbonate dissolution and soil CO₂ degassing following fresh water inflow45. Blue neurons predominantly indicate areas of low pH influenced by CO₂ accumulation and silicate weathering38, and neurons shifting from red to blue after monsoon suggest intensification of these processes in certain locations. The widespread variability in pH during post-monsoon points to significant changes in the geochemical processes controlling groundwater pH. Limited correlation between pH and HCO₃⁻ weight planes and wide variation in pH weight plane in both seasons indicate multiple factors beyond carbonate or silicate weathering govern groundwater pH.

The TDS weight planes exhibit a consistent neuron pattern strongly correlated with TH, Ca2⁺, Mg2⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, and SO₄2⁻, confirming their collective role in groundwater salinization. The notable shift in high-weight neuron positions from pre- to post-monsoon (Fig. 3a and b) indicates dilution of pre-existing saline zones by freshwater inflow and subsequent formation of new saline pockets through displacement of residual saline water.

The NO₃⁻ weight plane shows a distinctly different pattern from TDS and associated ions, suggesting a source independent from the salinization processes. During pre-monsoon, NO₃⁻ distribution appears localized (Fig. 3a), whereas post-monsoon shows scattered high-weight neurons, indicating increased and scattered anthropogenic sources after monsoonal recharge (Fig. 3b). Additionally, localized regions (BR) with concurrent peaks in TDS, pH, HCO₃⁻, and NO₃⁻ during post-monsoon reflect anthropogenic activities influencing salinity, alkalinity, and pH simultaneously.

The fluoride (F-) weight planes differ markedly from those of TDS and associated ions, indicating fluoride release is largely independent of salinity. High-weight fluoride zones remain relatively stable across both seasons, shifting marginally toward saline regions post-monsoon. This minimal seasonal variation aligns well with Kruskal–Wallis test results (Table S3). However, closer proximity of high fluoride zones to areas of elevated NO₃⁻ and TDS during post-monsoon, coupled with fluoride’s stronger correlation with pH compared to HCO₃⁻, indicates a potential increase in fluoride leaching influenced by anthropogenic or salinity-driven changes in groundwater pH after the monsoon.

Based on K-means clustering and CHI as well as Elbow indices, total 5 and 3 clusters were obtained during pre- and post-monsoon seasons respectively (Fig. S15, S16S17, Fig. 4a, b and Table S5). Clusters were overlaid on U-matrix output of the SOM analysis based on HCA of neuron weights (Fig. S16). The z-score–based cluster profiling and point-centered buffer overlays were applied to identify the dominant variables of each cluster (Table S5) and to extract the prevailing LULC and geological features controlling groundwater chemistry within 500 m buffer radius of the wells respectively (Fig. 5, Fig. S16 and S17). Based on the results, pre-monsoon clustering -revealed five hydrochemical regimes strongly influenced by lithology and land use. Cluster 1 was defined by elevated fluoride (2.5–6.5 mg/L) with Na–HCO₃ facies, arising in caliche-rich alluvium, Granite/Granite Gneiss derived clay units around rural settlements (Table S5, Fig. 5). Here, calcite precipitation depleted Ca2⁺, enhancing fluoride solubility, while semi-arid soils and long residence times promoted water–rock interaction and F- enrichment. This cluster can be defined as “Geogenic control belt”. Cluster 2 showed moderate TDS and hardness, low fluoride (0.02 to 1.95 mg/L), and elevated nitrate, typical of agricultural alluvium where irrigation recharge diluted salts but introduced fertilizer-derived NO₃⁻. Importantly, the Ca- and laterite-bearing geology in this cluster provided a natural fluoride “buffer,” as abundant Ca2⁺ limited F- mobility through CaF₂ precipitation46 (Fig. 5). The cluster can be termed as “Anthropogenic fingerprint belt”. Cluster 3 comprised hypersaline Na–Cl–SO₄ waters with TDS often > 5000 mg/L but low fluoride (0.32 to 0.82 mg/L), representing coastal/deltaic aquifers influenced by seawater intrusion and aquaculture-based land cover. This cluster mostly represent “Localised saline pockets”. Cluster 4 (Fig. 5) contained moderately saline, very hard waters (TDS 1000–3000 mg/L, TH > 400 mg/L), often sulfate-rich due to evaporative concentration in inland alluvium with poor drainage and scrub–aquaculture land use. Despite elevated salinity, fluoride mostly remained controlled (0.08 to 1.84 mg/L) by high Ca2⁺ availability. This cluster represent “Rock interaction and anthropogenic induced salinization”. Cluster 5 represented the freshest waters (TDS 100–300 mg/L) with slightly acidic to neutral pH and uniformly low fluoride (0.08 to 2.30 mg/L). These Ca–Mg–HCO₃ type groundwaters were linked to lateritic uplands and piedmont recharge zones, where rapid flushing and Ca-rich laterite soils scavenged fluoride, ensuring safe concentrations even under semi-arid conditions (Fig. 5). This cluster was defined as the “Background” level of groundwater with minimal contamination.Fig. 4
(a) K-means clustered samples superimposed on LULC study area during pre- and post-monsoon seasons. (b) K-means clustered samples superimposed on lithology of study area during pre- and post-monsoon seasons.Fig. 5
K-means cluster wise geology and LULC composition during pre- and post-monsoon season.

During the post-monsoon season, the hydrogeochemical system contracted into three dominant groups (Fig. S15 and S16). Cluster 1 persisted as the high-fluoride group (0.02 to 7.10 mg/L), merging not only pre-monsoon Cluster 1 but also some samples from pre-monsoon cluster 5 (Table S5). Seasonal recharge mobilized additional fluoride from soil and sediment, while calcite precipitation continued to strip Ca2⁺, preventing natural attenuation. Cluster 2 merged the former agricultural (pre-monsoon Cluster 2), transitional (pre-monsoon Cluster 4), and part of the fresh (pre-monsoon cluster 5) waters, producing low-fluoride group (0.12 to 2.80 mg/L) with fewer samples exceeding 1.5 mg/L limit. It is characterized by variable nitrate, hardness, and sulfate with average F- concentration of 0.89 mg/L. This outcome underscores the stabilizing effect of lateritic soils and Ca-bearing sediments, which scavenged fluoride even when recharge flushed other solutes into the system (Fig. 5). Cluster 3 remained the hypersaline end-member, unchanged from pre-monsoon, reflecting coastal hydrogeology dominated by seawater intrusion and marshy aquaculture land use where high ionic strength and abundant Ca2⁺ naturally suppressed fluoride solubility (0.59 to 0.98 mg/L).

sec.title: Identification of hydrological sources based on PCA
sec.p: Sampling adequacy for PCA was confirmed by KMO statistics of 0.75 (pre-monsoon) and 0.74 (post-monsoon), both within the acceptable range (Table S6).

Bartlett’s test of sphericity was highly significant in both cases (χ2 = 3903.1 and 3659.8, p < 0.001 for pre- and post-monsoon seasons respectively) (Table S6), indicating sufficient intercorrelation of variables and proving applicability of the PCA technique. According to the Scree plots (Fig. S18), first five PCs explaining over 90% variance of the groundwater chemistry data were selected for further interpretation of major geochemical process and Bayesian APCS-MLR source apportionment (Fig. 6a, 6b, Table S7). The varimax rotation took 7 iterations for convergence. The final varimax rotated loading values for first five PCs during both pre- and post-monsoon season are provided in Fig. 6a, 6b.Fig. 6
(a, b) pre- and post-monsoon varimax rotated factor loadings of first 5 PCs; (c) Results of Bayesian-APCS-MLR showing different source/process contributions with 95% uncertainty intervals.

Based on the loading values, the PC1 factor during pre-monsoon season (Fig. 6a) indicate geogenic salinity–hardness factor. PC1 loads positively and near uniformly on TDS, TH, Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, K+, Cl⁻ and SO42- (loading values 0.27 to 0.39), marking a broad water rock interaction axis controlling groundwater salinity and hardness. In coastal reaches, the same axis also defines seawater influence/evaporative concentration. Empirically, pre-monsoon Cluster 3 (coastal/aquaculture–mangrove settings) shows very high PC1 alongside extreme TDS (~ up to 14 g/L), while upland fresher waters (e.g., Cluster 5) fall along low PC1 scores. In short, PC1 is a salinity–hardness gradient dominated by geogenic dissolution, with seawater mixing and evaporation acting as localised factors (Fig. S19, S21).

PC2 represents pH modulating reactions with almost a pure pH axis (loading ≈ 0.98) (Fig. 6a), defining the acid–base geochemical changes caused by the CO₂–carbonate buffer and other processes impacting pH of local groundwater system. High PC2 scores indicate alkaline, well-buffered waters, representative of carbonate-bearing alluvium and irrigated fields where carbonate dissolution or liming results increasing pH upward (e.g., modestly positive in Cluster 2). Negative PC2 scores shows acidic conditions where buffering is weak or soil CO₂ is high which is consistent with lateritic/granitic terrains (Cluster 5, Fig. S20, S22). The control is fundamentally geogenic (mineralogy and dissolved inorganic carbon) but is clearly controlled by land use and irrigation return flow which is evident from the box plot of PC2 scores vs. geological and LULC components (Fig. S20). In practical terms, PC2 governs speciation and solubility (e.g., metals, fluoride), making it a dominating variable for downstream reactions even when other ions contribute little to this component.

PC3 defines mainly anthropogenic sources with dominating nitrate axis (loading ≈ 0.99) (Fig. 6a) and minimal co-loadings, cleanly isolating human-derived NO₃⁻ inputs from geogenic sources. High PC3 scores coincide with wells in intensively farmed plains (Cluster 2; crop-land/rural LULC), where measured NO₃⁻ is ~ 20–40 mg/L consistent with fertilizer leaching and, locally, septic effluent (Fig. S19). Forested/low-density areas plot strongly negative on PC3, reflecting background NO₃⁻ levels (Fig. S19).

PC4 characterises the geogenic fluoride release with almost entirely defined by fluoride (F- loading ≈ 0.99) (Fig. 6a). The geology data show that samples with elevated F- (high PC4 scores) often falls along areas underlain by granitic/gneissic rocks or weathered alluvium formations (Fig. S19) for example, some Cluster 4 and Cluster 1 sites have F- of 3–6 mg/L and high PC4 scores, aligning with known high F- geologies (Fig. S19, S21). Land use is not a direct driver of fluoride, with most high PC4 scores falling in built up areas with intensive groundwater usage (Fig. S19). High fluoride often co-occurs with long residence times and high alkalinity; however, in this case fluoride emerged as an independent factor (minimal cross loading with HCO₃⁻ in pre-monsoon), suggesting localized geologic control.

PC5 mainly designates the recharge induced silicate weathering factor controlling groundwater alkalinity (Bicarbonate Factor) with strong loading for HCO₃⁻ (–0.91) (Fig. 6a). This inverse loading means that higher bicarbonate in a sample corresponds to a lower PC5 score (and low HCO₃⁻ yields high PC5 score). PC5 distinguishes waters dominated by carbonate dissolution vs. those by silicate weathering or ion exchange. For instance, samples in carbonate-rich alluvial areas (high HCO₃⁻) have negative PC5, whereas those in non-carbonate hard-rock areas (lower HCO₃⁻) show positive PC5 (Fig. S19, S21). Indeed, upland Cluster 5 wells (in laterite/granite, which yield low alkalinity water) have some of the highest PC5 scores, reflecting their low bicarbonate content. By contrast, Cluster 4 and 1 wells in valley/alluvial settings (which accumulate HCO₃⁻ from calcite/dolomite dissolution) have strongly negative PC5 scores (Fig. S19, S21). This factor is primarily geogenic but differentiates aquifer lithologies.

During post-monsoon season, similar to pre-monsoon, PC1 remains geogenic salinity–hardness factor with comparable loading values for TDS, Ca2⁺, Mg2⁺, K⁺, SO₄2⁻, and TH (loadings ~ 0.34–0.48) and to a lesser degree Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (0.24 and 0.21 respectively) (Fig. 6b). This indicates that although halite type salinity is reduced, alkaline earths and sulfate remain dominant which is consistent with dilution of marine salt influence by fresh rainwater. Samples in coastal cluster groups still score high on PC1 post-monsoon, indicating residual salinity, but overall TDS values decline post-monsoon, redistributing some variance to other factors (Fig. S20, S21).

PC2 during post monsoon remains pH modulating factor with pH loading value of 0.96 (Fig. 6b). The heavy monsoon recharge can change CO₂ dynamics and soil leaching, but overall, the pH factor persisted. For example, samples from lateritic areas (pre-monsoon Cluster 5) remain more acidic (negative PC2 scores post-monsoon), whereas from areas with carbonate or anthropogenic inputs remain more alkaline (positive PC2) (Fig. S19-S22).

The PC3 during post-monsoon season characterises the geogenic fluoride release component with high loading value of fluoride (0.99) suggesting that fluoride leaching phenomenon becomes statistically more significant after monsoon period. Like pre-monsoon season the high PC3 score zones during post-monsoon season aligns with fluoride dominated granitic gneiss and derived alluvium deposit lithological units (Fig. S20).

The PC4 component during post-monsoon represents anthropogenic sources like pre monsoon PC3 component. The component is characterised by NO3⁻ (loading 0.99) axis, however, decrease in explained variance of the anthropogenic component during post-monsoon season reflects how dilution and perhaps uptake by crops during monsoon reduced the overall variance of nitrate relative to other factors (dropping it from PC3 to PC4 in rank) (Fig. 6b, Fig. S20, S22). Several Cluster 2 wells (pre-monsoon) still show high NO3⁻ in post-monsoon sampling with some even higher than pre-monsoon. The geological units show dominance of alluvium deposits with builtup, agricultural cropland and aquaculture pond aligning with high PC4 zones (Fig. S20).

PC5 during the post-monsoon season reflects recharge-driven silicate weathering and alkalinity control (HCO₃⁻ loading 0.77). Moderate Na⁺ (~ 0.34) and Cl⁻ (~ 0.38) loadings, along with a negative SO₄2⁻ (–0.35) (Fig. 6b), indicate carbonic-acid weathering of feldspars and micas during CO₂-rich recharge, releasing Na⁺ and HCO₃⁻ while diluting or reducing SO₄2⁻, and shifting waters toward Na–HCO₃ facies. High PC5 scores in sand, silt & gravel and sand–silt–clay formations confirm this, as these porous alluvia favour longer flow paths and active weathering (Fig. S20). Conversely, lateritic soils and dolerite/granophyre units show low scores, consistent with shallow weathering and rapid runoff. Land-use patterns reinforce this trend: agriculture–aquaculture and plantations record the highest PC5 due to enhanced infiltration and soil CO₂, while forested and riverine areas remain near zero, reflecting low residence times and bicarbonate dilution.

Overall PC1, PC4 (pre)/PC3 (post) are dominantly geogenic factors representing salinisation and fluoride leaching respectively, PC2 and PC5 show mixed control of both geology and LULC representing pH condition and recharge induced silicate weathering/ion exchange process and PC3 (pre)/PC4 (post) is purely anthropogenic component.

sec.title: Source apportionment using Bayesian-APCS-MLR modelling
sec.p: The Bayesian model findings (Table S8 and Fig. 6c) suggest that geogenic fluoride sources (PC4) were the dominant contributor in the region, with an average estimated contribution of 89.14% (95% CI 80.09–97.26%) during the pre-monsoon season. Other factors, such as the pH factor (PC2), were associated with a comparatively minor contribution of 4.48% (CI 0.32–9.19%), followed by recharge-induced silicate weathering and alkalinity control (PC5), which showed an estimated contribution of 1.24% (CI 0.12–2.39%). The geogenic salinity factor (PC1) and anthropogenic factor (PC3) were estimated to have negligible contributions (< 1%) to groundwater fluoride contamination. In the post-monsoon period, the geogenic fluoride factor (PC3) remained the dominant contributor to groundwater F-, accounting for about 48.86% (CI 38.80–64.91%), while the pH factor (PC2) showed a substantial auxiliary association (16.13%, CI 3.20–24.11%) (Fig. 6c). The anthropogenic source factor (PC4) accounted for only 0.53% (CI 0.02–1.48%) of F-, which is consistent with limited direct anthropogenic influence on fluoride mass despite agricultural effects on other solutes. Recharge-induced silicate weathering and ion exchange (PC5) showed an average contribution of 3.83% (CI 0.75–7.31%), whereas the salinity–hardness factor (PC1) remained negligibly associated (0.61%, CI 0.03–1.54%). The contribution from unidentified sources increased from 4.77% (CI 0.35–9.23%) in the pre-monsoon season to 30.03% (CI 24.72–33.68%) in the post-monsoon season.

Overall, pre-monsoon fluoride contamination in the study area is predominantly linked to direct geogenic leaching, contributing nearly 89% (Fig. 6c). During the dry season, prolonged groundwater residence time enhances interaction with fluoride-bearing minerals, while low Ca2⁺ concentrations, caused by calcite precipitation and Ca2⁺–Na⁺ cation exchange, shift fluorite dissolution equilibrium forward and increase F- release. As a result, these waters commonly evolve toward a Na–HCO₃ facies with elevated pH and reduced divalent cations. Post-monsoon, the controlling mechanisms become more diverse. The geogenic fluoride contribution declines sharply to ~ 49% (Fig. 6c), mainly due to dilution by fresh recharge and increased Ca2⁺ from carbonate dissolution. This produces a common-ion effect that suppresses fluoride solubility by stabilizing fluorite saturation. At the same time, pH-modulating processes increase about fourfold (~ 16%), indicating stronger control by soil CO₂, bicarbonate buffering, and pH-driven sorption–desorption dynamics. Recharge-induced silicate weathering and ion exchange also intensify, with their contribution rising about threefold to ~ 4% after monsoon. This is attributed to Ca–Na exchange on aquifer clays, which reduces Ca2⁺ availability and enhances Na⁺, promoting a Na–HCO₃ hydrochemical character. Where this process is strong, the loss of Ca2⁺ may offset the common-ion suppression of fluoride and allow its re-mobilization despite ongoing recharge. However, this pathway remains secondary to the broader influence of the carbonate system. Contributions from anthropogenic and geogenic salinity components remain minimal in both seasons, indicating a minimal direct role of these factors in controlling groundwater fluoride geochemistry.

The unidentified contribution, which increased to ~ 30% during post-monsoon, was interpreted as a physically meaningful residual component rather than simple statistical noise. It can be considered to reflect processes not fully resolved by the linear PCA-based APCS-MLR framework, particularly non-linear geochemical reactions involved in fluoride mobilisation, such as pH-dependent desorption, ion exchange, and mineral dissolution–precipitation behaviour that cannot be adequately represented by orthogonal linear components. Depth-dependent mixing within the stratified aquifer system is also considered plausible, as individual samples may integrate shallow and deeper waters with contrasting hydrochemical signatures. Colloidal or complexed fluoride is regarded as a possible but secondary contributor, although this cannot be verified without dedicated speciation or filtration data. Seasonal changes in hydraulic connectivity is also an important factor contributing to unidentified fraction, because recharge pulses and shifting groundwater–surface water interactions can alter flow paths and geochemical conditions between seasons. More broadly, this behaviour highlights the inferential limits of receptor modelling, whereby source contributions are inferred from statistical patterns at the sampling point and therefore represent probable associations rather than direct proof of causality, especially where sources overlap, important controls remain unmeasured, or aquifer behaviour is non-linear. Moreover, Structural uncertainties related to PC retention, component stability, Varimax rotation, and limited process resolution may further contribute to the unidentified fraction. Uncertainty was found to widen post-monsoon, particularly in coastal samples and the unidentified share, indicating the need for seasonally adaptive monitoring and model updating in higher-uncertainty zones.

sec.title: Role of geology and LULC on seasonality of fluoride geochemistry
sec.p:
Groundwater chemistry across the study area showed a strong association between geological texture and LULC, with distinct pre- and post-monsoon signatures (Fig. 10, Fig. S23 and S24). In the pre-monsoon season, fine-textured formations, including yellowish-brown fine sand–silt–clay, generic sand–silt–clay, and laterite, showed fluoride-dominated geochemistry, with geogenic fluoride (PC4) contributing on average 93.68%, 91.90%, and 91.54%, respectively (Fig. 10a, Fig. S23). This pattern was similarly observed in plantation, cropland, and built-up rural LULC types, with geogenic fluoride contributions of 93.96%, 90.01%, and 90.00% (Fig. 10g, Fig. S23). These conditions are consistent with low-permeability settings and long groundwater residence times that promote sustained water–rock interaction, while clays may act as temporary reservoirs that later release fluoride under compaction and stress47,48. Coarse alluvial deposits (sand–silt–gravel, SSG) showed a slightly more mixed signature, although the pre-monsoon geogenic fluoride factor still accounted for 85.72% (PC4), and pH-modulating factors (PC2) were more pronounced than in finer formations (5.78%) (Fig. 10b).Fig. 10
Source contribution variations across geological units (a–f: a – geogenic fluoride leaching, b – pH-controlling reactions, c – silicate weathering and ion exchange, d – salinisation processes, e – anthropogenic sources, f – unidentified sources) and across land-use/land-cover (LULC) classes (g–l: g – geogenic fluoride leaching, h – pH-controlling reactions, i – silicate weathering and ion exchange, j – salinisation processes, k – anthropogenic sources, l – unidentified sources) for pre- and post-monsoon seasons, respectively.

Following the monsoon, a marked chemical shift was observed. Geogenic fluoride contributions (PC3) declined but remained dominant, with fine-textured units recording PC3 shares of 66.99% in yellowish-brown fine sand–silt–clay and 52.96%, 48.44%, and 46.64% in oxidised sand-silt–clay with caliche nodules, sand–silt–clay, and laterite, respectively (Fig. 10a). In plantation land use, geogenic fluoride sources declined from ~ 94% pre-monsoon to 59.52% post-monsoon. Croplands and built-up areas showed similar reductions, with cropland at 45.04% and built-up categories at 51–55% (core urban 51.30%, peri-urban 55.44%, rural mixed 52.77%), while rural village was 36.13%, yet geogenic fluoride leaching remained the dominant process (Fig. 10g). This decline was accompanied by higher pH-modulating reactions, with PC2 rising to 10.69–17.15% in fine-textured geologies (fine sand–silt–clay 10.69%, sand–silt–clay 14.60%, laterite 17.15%), ~ 14–21% in cropland and built-up areas (cropland 17.69%; built-up rural village 21.13%), and 11.85% in plantation areas (Fig. 10h). Silicate weathering and cation exchange also became more important, with PC5 increasing to ~ 2.32–4.31% across these classes (e.g., sand–silt–clay 4.31%; fine sand–silt–clay 2.32%) (Fig. 10b).

The strongest seasonal transitions were observed in coarse alluvium and surface-water-linked LULC types. In SSG, geogenic fluoride contributions declined to 39.22% (PC3), whereas the pH factor rose to 19.04% (PC2) (Fig. 10a, b) and silicate weathering/exchange averaged 4.99% (PC5) (Fig. 10c). Post-monsoon, lakes and ponds showed pH reactions contributing 19.66% (PC2) (Fig. 10h) and silicate weathering/exchange 5.25% (PC5) (Fig. 10i), while aquaculture areas showed similar values of 19.35% (PC2) and 7.28% (PC5) (Fig. 10h, i). Leakage from aquaculture ponds, rich in bicarbonate and nutrients, likely intensified carbonate buffering, pH changes, and cation exchange, resulting in localized fluoride redistribution17. Although moderated, the geogenic fluoride leaching factor (PC3) remained important, contributing ~ 34–36% across these surface-linked LULC classes (lakes/ponds 34.56%, aquaculture 35.85%) (Fig. 10g). These patterns are consistent with rapid recharge, bank infiltration, and shallow mixing processes.

Geologies with caliche nodules or calcareous concretions responded strongly to recharge, showing post-monsoon PC2 means of 16.28% (oxidised sand–silt–clay with caliche nodules) and 16.45% (sand–silt–clay with calcareous concretions) (Fig. 10b). These pH changes were intensified adjacent to aquaculture and pond settings, highlighting the synergy between lithology and surface-water-linked land cover. Salinity contributions (PC1) remained consistently low, ranging from ~ 0.06–0.39% pre-monsoon across common LULC/geology classes (e.g., SSG 0.24%, plantation 0.33%, lakes 0.13%) to ~ 0.30–1.76% post-monsoon (e.g., SSG 1.01%, plantation 1.76%, lakes 1.57%) (Fig. 10d, j). Anthropogenic nitrate (PC3 pre- and PC4 post-monsoon) was similarly minor; pre-monsoon PC3 was typically ~ 0.02–1.30% across LULC (most classes < 0.60%), and post-monsoon PC4 remained ~ 0.02–1.81% (highest in wasteland dense scrub and “Others – Rann”) (Fig. 10e, k).

Taken together, the results demonstrated that geogenic fluoride factor (≈ 86–96% pre-monsoon and 35–67% post-monsoon across all geological features) was consistently strongest in fine-textured geologies and plantation/cropland/built-up settings (Fig. 10a, g). Monsoon recharge systematically reduced geogenic fluoride contributions while enhancing pH modulating reactions (PC2 up to ~ 21% in built-up and ~ 20% in aquaculture/lakes) (Fig. 10b, h) and silicate weathering/cation exchange (PC5 typically ~ 3–7%, higher in some surface-linked classes) (Fig. 10c, i). These shifts were most pronounced where permeable alluvium overlapped with surface-connected LULC, leading to rapid infiltration and strong groundwater–surface water mixing, which is also evident from depth variation of fluoride concentration in the study area (Fig. S25). In contrast, fine-textured and plantation zones retained geogenic fluoride sources as the primary control but still gained modest pH changes and silicate weathering/cation exchange signatures with fresh recharge. Seasonality in groundwater chemistry in this region therefore is a function of recharge-driven changes, with aquaculture leakage and clay compaction providing probable pathways for fluoride release superimposed on a persistent geogenic baseline.

Given this dynamically evolving hydrochemical setting, future methodological improvement may lie in adaptive learning frameworks that can update feature representations in response to changing system states, rather than relying only on fixed or pre-specified relationships; reinforcement-learning like approaches offer this advantage by learning task-specific feature combinations from the data environment through reward-guided feedback and have shown improved sensitivity to dynamic environmental signals in other monitoring contexts49,50.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Groundwater fluoride contamination in the coastal aquifer showed a clear seasonal variation in source dominance and process interaction. The Bayesian APCS-MLR model indicated that pre-monsoon fluoride was overwhelmingly geogenic (89.14%, 95% CI: 80.09–97.26%), with only minor contributions from pH modulation (4.48%, CI: 0.32–9.19%) and silicate weathering/cation exchange (1.24%, CI: 0.12–2.39%). Anthropogenic and salinity influences were negligible (0.23%, CI: 0.01–0.65%; 0.14%, CI: 0.01–0.42%, respectively). In the post-monsoon period, geogenic control declined to 48.86% (95% CI: 38.80–64.91%), while pH effects increased to 16.13% (CI: 3.20–24.11%) and ion-exchange contributions rose to 3.83% (CI: 0.75–7.31%). Unidentified contributions also increased sharply to 30.03% (CI: 24.72–33.68%), reflecting greater process overlap under post-monsoon conditions. Spatially, fine-textured formations and cropland or plantation areas remained strongly geogenic controlled during pre-monsoon (~ 90–94%), whereas coarse alluvium and aquaculture-linked zones showed stronger post-monsoon influence of pH variation and ion exchange.

These findings support a process-informed remediation framework for fluoride mitigation in coastal aquifers. In fine-textured laterite and sand–silt–clay formations, and in cropland, plantation, and rural settlement areas where geogenic fluoride remains dominant, priority should be given to point-of-use defluoridation, calcium-balanced blending, and nutritional support for vulnerable groups, particularly infants and children. In coarse alluvium and pond- or aquaculture-linked settings, where post-monsoon pH variation and ion exchange become more important, remediation should emphasize better pond lining, controlled recharge, and calcium re-equilibration. Managed aquifer recharge should be limited to shallow systems with proven dilution capacity and avoided in caliche-bearing formations. Seasonal health-risk mapping can further support adaptive interventions, including safe water supply planning, household defluoridation, caries management, and nutrition-based measures.
